_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 6 specification: one article, six gaps, SEVEN sentences A–G, one of them extra. Each removed sentence hooks backwards by reference (their, it, these decisions, even, he) and forwards to the next sentence (the governors said yes, their complaints, it took a full year, the pumpkins, though, his attendance). The extra sentence (C) tempts gap 2 because it is about teachers and their cars, but it says the staff were happy, so 'Their complaints' in the next sentence has nothing to refer to. Used by the Part 6 practice page and by Full test 5.
title: From tarmac to tomatoes
subtitle: When a secondary school dug up its only car park, the teachers had to walk. The students got a farm.
text: Three years ago, the staff car park at Hollins Lane School was a grey rectangle of cracked tarmac with spaces for forty cars. Today it produces enough vegetables to supply the school kitchen for much of the summer term. The idea came not from the head teacher but from a group of thirteen-year-olds, who wrote to the school governors after a science lesson on how far food travels before it is eaten. {1} The governors, somewhat to everyone's surprise, said yes.

Not everyone was pleased. The car park was the only one on the site, and the nearest public one was a ten-minute walk away, up a steep hill. {2} Their complaints were understandable, says Rachel Dunmore, the deputy head who oversaw the project, but most were quietly dropped after the first harvest. 'It is hard to stay angry,' she says, 'with someone who has just handed you a bag of free courgettes.'

Digging up the tarmac turned out to be the easy part. A local building firm removed it in a single weekend at no cost, in exchange for a sign with its name at the school gate. The soil underneath, however, was hard, grey and almost lifeless after decades under parked cars. {3} It still took a full year, and several hundred bags of compost donated by parents, before anything worth eating would grow.

The garden is now run almost entirely by students. Each year group is responsible for its own beds, and a committee of older students decides what to plant and when. {4} The pumpkins sold out in under an hour, however, and the money paid for a small greenhouse, which the younger students now admit was worth all the effort.

Teachers have also found uses for the garden that nobody had planned. Maths classes measure the growth of bean plants, history students have grown the vegetables that Victorian factory workers would have eaten, and the art department holds lessons there whenever the weather allows. {5} For some students, though, the most important lessons have nothing to do with the timetable.

Rachel Dunmore points to a boy in Year 9 who rarely spoke in class and was often absent. Two years ago he began staying after school to water the beds, and he is now in charge of the tomatoes. {6} His attendance, she adds, has not been this good since primary school.

Not everything has worked. Slugs destroyed an entire crop of lettuces in the first summer, and a fox has developed a worrying taste for strawberries. The teachers, meanwhile, still park in the street, and still walk up the hill in the rain. Asked whether she misses her old parking space, Rachel Dunmore laughs. 'Every wet Monday morning,' she says. 'And then I have lunch.'
sentences: Their decisions are not always popular: last year's plan to grow sixty pumpkins for a Halloween sale was called 'ridiculous' by the younger students who had to water them.
Several teachers, some of whom drove in from villages with no bus service, objected strongly.
Most of the teachers, however, welcomed the chance to leave their cars at home.
Even the music department has joined in, recording the sounds of the garden at different times of day for a composition project.
Their letter asked a simple question: why did the school's carrots travel further each day than most of its teachers?
He knows every plant by name, and visitors who touch them without asking are politely but firmly told off.
To bring it back to life, students built raised beds and filled them with leaves collected from the local park.
why: 'Their letter' is the one the thirteen-year-olds wrote; the governors then 'said yes' to its question.

The teachers who drove in from villages objected; 'their complaints' in the next sentence are these objections. C is on topic but says the staff were happy, so 'their complaints' would have nothing to refer to.
'It' is the lifeless soil; 'still took a full year' shows the raised beds alone were not enough.
'Their decisions' are the committee's; 'the pumpkins' and 'however' answer the younger students' complaint.
'Even the music department' adds one more subject to the list; 'though' then turns from school subjects to other lessons.
'He' is the boy now in charge of the tomatoes; 'his attendance' continues the description of him.
